claims.claim: People with ADHD discount delayed rewards much more steeply than others, so an exam grade nine months away carries far less motivational weight for her than it would for a typical student.
claims.source_title: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder and Monetary Delay Discounting: A Meta-Analysis of Case-Control Studies
claims.key_numbers: Search summary reports 'very strong evidence of significantly higher discounting of future rewards in ADHD' at p < 10^-15; pooled effect size and number of studies not shown in search summary.
claims.implication: The tutor skills should stop treating the May/June 2027 exams as the motivator; every session needs a proximal, visible payoff (an exit-ticket score, a topic status change, a personal best on the chart) delivered inside the session. The dashboard's 'N days to the exam' countdown is a parent planning figure and should not be the child's headline number.

claims.claim: In ADHD the pull towards small immediate rewards is amplified when the reward is real rather than hypothetical, so notional or promised rewards are especially weak motivators for her.
claims.source_title: ADHD and the Choice of Small Immediate Over Larger Delayed Rewards: A Comparative Meta-Analysis of Performance on Simple Choice-Delay and Temporal Discounting Paradigms
claims.key_numbers: 37 group comparisons (22 simple-choice, 15 temporal-discounting), N = 3,763 (53% ADHD); small-to-medium effect sizes for both paradigms; offering real rewards in the simple-choice paradigm 'almost doubled the odds ratio' for ADHD participants.
claims.implication: Feedback inside the system should be concrete and experienced at once (a score that appears, a chart that updates the moment a run is logged), not promised ('this will help in May'). The Shooting Gallery's instant score and the gold star are on the right side of this; tutor lines like 'this will matter for your grade' are on the wrong side.

claims.claim: ADHD behaviour is partly driven by delay aversion, a motivational drive to escape the unpleasant experience of waiting, which is separate from executive-function deficits and affects some but not all people with ADHD.
claims.source_title: The dual pathway model of AD/HD: An elaboration of neuro-developmental characteristics
claims.key_numbers: Theoretical model paper; no pooled effect size. Later work ('Beyond the Dual Pathway Model', JAACAP 2010) adds a third, timing-related pathway.
claims.implication: Long uninterrupted stretches (the 30-40 minute teach block, a long Claude explanation, a 90-minute session) are themselves aversive. Her 'skip it', 'I can't', answering every part at once, and leaving Q4/Q5 unsubmitted are consistent with delay escape, so the maths skill should shorten each teach-practise-feedback loop and make waits visible and finite ('two more questions, then the exit ticket').

claims.claim: Children with ADHD respond poorly to reinforcement that is delayed or intermittent, and immediate, frequent reward or response-cost feedback can improve their task performance more than it does for other children.
claims.source_title: The impact of reinforcement contingencies on AD/HD: a review and theoretical appraisal
claims.key_numbers: Narrative review, Clinical Psychology Review 25:183-213. Search summary: 'some evidence that appropriate motivational stimulation (such as reward or response cost) may improve cognitive functioning to a larger extent in children with ADHD than in controls', but 'only some studies report disproportional improvement'; children with ADHD prefer small immediate over larger delayed rewards; no pooled effect size.
claims.implication: In maths sessions, right/wrong-plus-what-to-fix feedback should follow each question immediately rather than being batched to the exit ticket or the end-of-session log, and any practice widget should return a result per item on submission, as the Shooting Gallery already does. Feedback frequency, not new game mechanics, is the ADHD-specific lever.

claims.claim: In a case-control experiment, children with ADHD showed a task-persistence deficit that disappeared under the strongest reinforcement condition, while their working memory improved but was not normalised.
claims.source_title: Can Motivation Normalize Working Memory and Task Persistence in Children with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder? The Effects of Money and Computer-Gaming
claims.authors_year: Dovis, Van der Oord, Wiers & Prins, 2012
claims.key_numbers: 86 children with ADHD vs 62 typically developing controls; feedback-only vs feedback + 10 euros; 'the strongest incentives normalized the persistence of performance in children with ADHD'; working memory improved but did not normalise. Case-control lab experiment, not a randomised trial.
claims.implication: Fading effort late in a session (unsubmitted Q4/Q5) is a motivational deficit that responds to salient reinforcement, not simply a discipline problem. Put the most visible, rewarding feedback at the end of the session (exit-ticket score shown at once, chart update), and have log_session record whether the session finished or ran out so the pattern becomes measurable.

claims.claim: Personal-best goals (aiming to beat your own previous performance) are positively associated with achievement and behavioural engagement in students with ADHD, about as strongly as in students without ADHD.
claims.source_title: The role of personal best (PB) goals in the achievement and behavioral engagement of students with ADHD and students without ADHD
claims.key_numbers: N = 3,374 students (ADHD and non-ADHD groups); multi-group multivariate path analysis found significant positive associations between PB goals and both achievement and behavioural engagement for students with ADHD, similar to non-ADHD; path coefficients not shown in search summary. Cross-sectional self-report, so causality is not established.
claims.implication: The personal-best gold star on her own chart is the one game-like element in the system with ADHD-specific supporting evidence and should be kept. Martin's work is about goals that are set, not just records that are displayed, so the tutor skills should state a personal-best target at the start of a session ('last exit ticket 22/25; today aim for 23, and zero blanks') and extend the framing to maths (fewest blanks, best exit-ticket score).

claims.claim: Expected tangible rewards for doing, finishing or performing well on a task undermine intrinsic motivation, whereas positive informational feedback increases it.
claims.source_title: A Meta-Analytic Review of Experiments Examining the Effects of Extrinsic Rewards on Intrinsic Motivation
claims.key_numbers: 128 experiments; engagement-, completion- and performance-contingent rewards undermined free-choice intrinsic motivation (d = -0.40, -0.36, -0.28); all tangible and all expected rewards undermined it; positive feedback enhanced free-choice behaviour (d = 0.33) and self-reported interest (d = 0.31).
claims.implication: A gold star that simply marks a personal best is closer to positive informational feedback than to a tangible contingent reward, so it is unlikely to undermine her interest. The risk appears if it becomes a currency (stars traded for privileges) or an expectation (a star every session); keep it informational, occasional and tied to her own data, and keep tutor praise specific to what she did rather than generic.

claims.claim: Intrinsic motivation is a medium-to-strong predictor of performance, matters more for the quality of work than its quantity, and predicts less when incentives are tied directly to performance.
claims.source_title: Intrinsic Motivation and Extrinsic Incentives Jointly Predict Performance: A 40-Year Meta-Analysis
claims.key_numbers: k = 183, N = 212,468 across school, work and physical domains; intrinsic motivation predicted performance at rho = .21-.45; moderator results for quality vs quantity and incentive contingency are described in the abstract but their numbers are not shown in search summary.
claims.implication: A GCSE grade is a quality outcome, so protecting her interest in maths and Spanish is a predictor of the result, not a soft extra. If the parent ever adds incentives, make them indirectly salient (for turning up, for finishing a session) rather than paid per mark or per topic secured.

claims.claim: Gamification produces small positive effects on learning, motivation and behaviour, but only the learning effect holds up when the analysis is restricted to methodologically rigorous studies.
claims.source_title: The Gamification of Learning: a Meta-analysis
claims.key_numbers: Cognitive g = 0.49 [0.30, 0.69], k = 19, N = 1,686; motivational g = 0.36 [0.18, 0.54], k = 16, N = 2,246; behavioural g = 0.25 [0.04, 0.46], k = 9, N = 951; cognitive effect stable in the high-rigor subsplit, motivational and behavioural effects 'less stable'.
claims.implication: Do not expect adding game mechanics to fix engagement; the defensible place for game-like design is inside the practice itself (the timed Shooting Gallery drill, retrieval starters with instant scoring), where the learning effect is the most robust part of the evidence. Judge any new feature by practice_stats accuracy and topic promotions, not by how fun it looks.

claims.claim: Learners say they value gamification for enthusiasm, performance feedback, recognition and goal-setting, but also report that it can cause anxiety or jealousy and sometimes adds nothing useful.
claims.source_title: Does gamification improve student learning outcome? Evidence from a meta-analysis and synthesis of qualitative data in educational contexts
claims.key_numbers: Hedges' g = 0.504 [0.284, 0.723], p < 0.001, 30 interventions from 24 quantitative studies, no publication bias detected; 32 qualitative studies gave four reasons for liking (enthusiasm, feedback on performance, recognition, goal setting) and two for disliking (no additional utility; anxiety or jealousy).
claims.implication: The elements the tracker keeps (immediate feedback, a personal record, an implicit goal) are the ones learners value; the elements it omits (comparison, streaks) are the ones behind the anxiety and jealousy complaints. This supports the README stance provided the chart stays about her own data and is never compared across subjects or with anyone else.

claims.claim: In a 16-week classroom comparison, adding badges and a leaderboard reduced students' intrinsic motivation, satisfaction and empowerment over time and lowered final exam scores through that drop in motivation.
claims.source_title: Assessing the effects of gamification in the classroom: A longitudinal study on intrinsic motivation, social comparison, satisfaction, effort, and academic performance
claims.key_numbers: Two university courses over a 16-week semester, one with leaderboard and badges; the gamified course showed less motivation, satisfaction and empowerment over time and lower final exam scores, mediated by intrinsic motivation; N not shown in search summary. Quasi-experiment with intact classes, not randomised.
claims.implication: Direct support for excluding badges and leaderboards from the tracker. It is a single quasi-experiment with university students, so it shows a real risk rather than proof of harm for this child; the stance is defensible on this evidence but should not be described as settled.

claims.claim: A logged streak becomes a goal in itself: an intact streak raises repeat engagement, but a broken one lowers it, most strongly when the person blames themselves for the break and least when the streak can be repaired.
claims.source_title: On or Off Track: How (Broken) Streaks Affect Consumer Decisions
claims.key_numbers: Seven randomised consumer experiments (not a clinical trial); streak defined as 3+ consecutive logged behaviours; effect independent of actual past behaviour and driven by how the log displays it; amplified for self-attributed breaks, attenuated when repair is possible; effect sizes not shown in search summary.
claims.implication: For a student whose inconsistency is a symptom rather than a choice, a streak display turns every missed day into a self-attributed failure with a measurable drop in follow-up engagement. The evidence supports the tracker's decision not to count consecutive days; if a consistency measure is ever wanted, use a rolling count ('3 sessions this week') that cannot be broken.

claims.claim: Game-based interventions for ADHD improve some laboratory cognitive measures (visuospatial short-term memory) but show no significant effect on inhibition or self-monitoring, so serious games should not be expected to treat ADHD symptoms or transfer to schoolwork.
claims.source_title: Efficacy of game-based interventions on cognitive performance in children and adolescents with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis
claims.authors_year: authors not shown in search summary; BMC Psychiatry, 2025
claims.key_numbers: 20 RCTs, 1,376 participants; significant improvement on Corsi Block Tapping Task forward (visuospatial short-term memory); effects on inhibition and monitoring not statistically significant; pooled effect sizes not shown in search summary.
claims.implication: Value the Spanish Shooting Gallery as vocabulary practice with immediate feedback, not as attention training, and do not divert study time to 'brain training' games in the hope of improving her maths attention. Judge the Gallery by its accuracy trend and by whether drilled vocabulary shows up in later reading and writing, which the tracker can check through topic refs on practice runs.

claims.claim: People are more motivated when progress feedback highlights whichever is smaller: accumulated progress early in a goal, remaining progress near the end.
claims.source_title: Small-Area Hypothesis: Effects of Progress Monitoring on Goal Adherence
claims.key_numbers: Series of randomised lab and field experiments (not clinical); early in goal pursuit '20% completed' beat '80% remaining', near the goal '20% remaining' beat '80% completed'; effect sizes and N not shown in search summary.
claims.implication: With maths at 23% conquered and Spanish at 1%, any child-facing view should foreground what has been secured (16 secure topics, 71-81% accuracy runs, blanks down from 27 marks to zero), not the 77% or 99% still to do. The 'N days to the exam' countdown and the '24 not started' count are to-go framings suited to the parent; switch the child's view to 'what is left' only in the final weeks before the May 2027 papers.

caveats: No study was found that tests a personal-best marker (gold star or similar) on a progress chart with adolescents with ADHD; C6 (Martin 2012) is about personal-best goals students set, measured by self-report and cross-sectional path analysis, not about a displayed record, so the gold star is supported by analogy rather than directly.

The delay-discounting meta-analyses (C1, C2) mostly use monetary choice tasks in the laboratory; the step from 'discounts money more steeply' to 'an exam nine months away is a weak motivator' is an inference consistent with the dual-pathway model, not a measured educational outcome.

The gamification meta-analyses (C9, C10, and Huang et al. 2020, g = 0.464 [0.244, 0.684], 30 studies, N = 3,083, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11423-020-09807-z) are general-population, mostly higher-education samples with short interventions; none stratifies by ADHD, and Sailer & Homner note the motivational effects are the least stable part.

Evidence against badges, leaderboards and streaks (C11, C12) is general-population: Hanus & Fox is one quasi-experiment with university students, and Silverman & Barasch studied consumers, not learners. A systematic review of leaderboards in higher education (Li et al. 2024, Journal of Computer Assisted Learning, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jcal.13077) appeared in results with a summary indicating lower-ranked students lose motivation, but its numbers could not be examined before the search budget ran out.

A February 2026 8-week RCT of a gamified educational app (immediate feedback, rewards, level-based challenges) versus a content-matched non-gamified app in 80 children aged 6-12 with diagnosed ADHD was found (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/398584473_Effectiveness_of_a_gamified_educational_application_on_attention_and_academic_performance_in_children_with_ADHD_an_8-week_randomized_controlled_trial) but its results were not shown in the search summary and the session's search budget was exhausted before a follow-up search; it is the closest direct test of gamified learning in ADHD and should be checked by a verifier.

A longitudinal study of gamification (Rodrigues et al. 2022, N = 756 STEM students over 14 weeks, https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1325797) reports a novelty effect: gamification's contribution fell after about four weeks and partially recovered between weeks six and ten. This is general-population but relevant to whether the Shooting Gallery's appeal will last; the tracker's practice log can show whether run frequency declines.

Mekler et al. 2017 (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0747563215301229) found points, levels and leaderboards raised the quantity of work done without changing intrinsic motivation, i.e. they acted as extrinsic incentives; this cuts against both the strongest pro- and anti-gamification claims and is general-population.

Luman et al. 2005 (C4) is a 20-year-old narrative review and its search summary is explicit that only some studies show disproportionate improvement with reward in ADHD; a 2021 systematic review of instrumental learning in ADHD (JAACAP, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0890856721001817) appeared in results but its findings were not shown.

Nothing was found on ADHD medication status or age moderating any of these effects at age 13 specifically; the ADHD samples in C1-C5 and C13 are mostly children under 12 or mixed-age, and C6's sample is high-school age.

Four planned searches (2026 RCT results, Li 2024 leaderboard review details, streaks in learning apps with adolescents, and 2023-2025 meta-analyses of gamification and self-determination theory) were blocked when the session hit its 200-search cap; the streak evidence in C12 is therefore from consumer research and the only streak-specific education sources returned were blog posts, which were not cited.
